body:
Yep—definitely acknowledged. If it can't be fixed, I wonder if it can be documented, or maybe the exception can be more verbose. I think my main concern is that El Capitan still ships with OpenSSL 0.9.8zg, and it's not really obvious from the stack trace what's going wrong.

One option: we could look for a `BEGIN PRIVATE KEY` and an `END PRIVATE KEY`, and complain about unexpected characters if the pattern doesn't match.
@normanmaurer - I would prefer not to support the "old ... non standard technique". However I have no strong objections if someone wants to submit a PR and maintain it.

@normanmaurer Sounds good to me. But we could somehow detect the old format and produce some helpful exception message? (e.g. you are using non-standard format. use `<some unix command>` to convert your private key)

@jchambers can you check if you can convert the generated file via:

```
openssl pkcs8 -in <PKCS#8 Key Filename> -out <Unencrypted Key Filename>
openssl pkcs8 -v1 PBE-SHA1-3DES -topk8 -in <Unencrypted Key Filename> -out <Encrypted Key Filename>
```

And then use the new generated file with netty ?

So basically like explained here:
http://help.globalscape.com/help/secureserver3/Converting_a_PEM_Encoded_PKCS_8_Format_Encrypted_private_key_to_a_compatible.htm

I just ran through those steps, and just converting to a PKCS#8-formatted key is enough to clear those headers (i.e. it doesn't look like we necessarily need to explicitly call out an algorithm).

That said, I think there may be another (masked?) issue at play here. From the [OpenSSL release notes](https://www.openssl.org/news/openssl-1.0.0-notes.html) (emphasis added):

> ## Major changes between OpenSSL 0.9.8n and OpenSSL 1.0.0 [29 Mar 2010]:
> - RFC3280 path validation: sufficient to process PKITS tests.
> - Integrated support for PVK files and keyblobs.
> - **Change default private key format to PKCS#8.**
> - …

So that means that the key I originally extracted with OpenSSL 0.9.8zg with:

```
openssl pkcs12 -in key.p12 -nocerts -out key.pem
```

…wasn't PKCS#8-encoded at all. It was in the "traditional format." So I guess this leaves me with two thoughts:
1. If we wind up with bonus headers in the private key block, we're probably not looking at a PKCS#8-formatted key at all, and explicitly converting to PKCS#8 will be enough to set things right both by way of removing the headers and by converting to the correct format (which I think would have surfaced as an issue if the headers weren't present).
2. My "traditional format" key began with `-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----`, while my PKCS#8-formatted key began with `-----BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY-----`. I haven't found anything in writing that says that PKCS#8-formatted keys will always begin with that string, but if we can build confidence that they do, that might be an easy way to detect this problem going forward.

So, yeah, @normanmaurer, looks good to me ;)
@jchambers ok cool. Let me just come up with some more useful exception message  then :)
